stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. runs a customer service agent named Agent1 in Foundry Agent Service. The operations team needs one indicator on the Agent Monitoring Dashboard that shows the percentage of agent runs that complete without failing, so that the team can open an investigation when the value drops below 95 percent.

Which dashboard metric should the team use?
choices: Red teaming results
Run success rate
Latency
Token usage
explanation: The Agent Monitoring Dashboard combines operational metrics (run success rate, latency, token usage) with quality and safety signals (evaluations, red teaming). Map the symptom to the metric: failures to run success rate, slowness to latency, cost to token usage, and safety to red teaming results.
rationale: Incorrect: red teaming results summarize adversarial scans that probe the agent for safety risks such as jailbreaks. They say nothing about how many production runs fail. Use them when you track safety exposure, not run health.

Correct: run success rate is the percentage of agent runs that complete without failing. It is the direct agent health indicator, and Microsoft Learn names a value below 95 percent as a reason to investigate failed runs.

Incorrect: latency shows how long runs take and points to throttling or slow tools. A run can be fast and still fail, so latency does not give the share of successful runs. Use it for a response-time objective.

Incorrect: token usage shows how many tokens runs consume and helps you spot verbose prompts or responses that drive cost. It does not show whether runs completed. Use it when you investigate cost or context growth.

stem:
Tailspin Toys has a multi-agent solution in which an orchestrator agent calls two subagents hosted in separate Azure Container Apps apps. All components send OpenTelemetry data to the same Application Insights resource. An engineer needs a KQL query that returns every request, dependency, and trace record that belongs to one end-to-end user transaction across the three components.

Which Application Insights field should the engineer filter on?
choices: The id field of the request telemetry
operation_Id
operation_ParentId
cloud_RoleName
explanation: Application Insights correlates distributed telemetry through the operation context: operation_Id is the trace ID shared by all items of one transaction, operation_ParentId links an item to its parent, and cloud_RoleName names the component. Filter on operation_Id for end-to-end views and on cloud_RoleName for per-component views.
rationale: Incorrect: the id field of a request item is unique to that one request, so filtering on it returns a single request and none of the dependency or trace records downstream. Use it when you need one specific request only.

Correct: operation_Id holds the W3C trace ID that every request, dependency, and trace item of one distributed transaction shares, so one filter returns the full path through the orchestrator and both subagents.

Incorrect: operation_ParentId points to the immediate parent of an item. Filtering on it returns only the direct children of one span, not the whole transaction. Use it when you rebuild the parent-child tree inside a trace.

Incorrect: cloud_RoleName identifies the component that emitted the telemetry, such as one Container Apps app. It returns every transaction of that component, not one transaction across all three. Use it to filter by service.

stem:
Wingtip Toys runs an orchestrator agent and four subagents as separate Azure Container Apps apps. Each app sends telemetry to one Application Insights resource with a distinct cloud role name. The operations team has three monitoring needs.

Which Application Insights feature should the team use for each need? To answer, drag the appropriate features to the correct needs. Each feature may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
choices: Application map
Live Metrics
Smart detection
Standard test
Workbooks
targets: Need1: a visual topology of the components and the calls between them, with failure hotspots per component
Need2: current request and failure rates while a new subagent version rolls out, without waiting for ingestion
Need3: an automatic notification when the failure rate rises abnormally compared with earlier days, without writing alert logic
explanation: Application Insights offers several views on the same telemetry: Application map for topology, Live Metrics for real time, smart detection for anomaly notification, Standard tests for synthetic availability, and workbooks for custom reporting. Match the feature to whether the need is structure, immediacy, detection, reachability, or reporting.
rationale: Need1 asks for topology with per-component health. Application map draws each cloud role name as a node and each call as an edge, and it highlights failing or slow nodes, which a test or a report does not do.

Need2 needs current numbers during a rollout. Live Metrics streams near real-time requests, failures, and dependency calls from the running apps, whereas the other features read stored telemetry or synthetic results.

Need3 needs anomaly-based notification with no rule to write. Smart detection learns the normal failure rate and alerts on abnormal rises, while a Standard test only checks whether an endpoint is reachable.
notes: Application map: a topology view built from telemetry with health KPIs per node. Use it to find which component or dependency causes failures in a distributed application.
Live Metrics: a near real-time stream of key telemetry from running instances. Use it during deployments or incidents when you must see the effect of a change immediately.
Smart detection: machine-learning detection of failure anomalies that needs no setup. Use it when thresholds are hard to choose because the normal failure rate varies with load.
Standard test: a synthetic availability test that calls a public URL from several locations and can validate TLS certificates. Use it to monitor reachability, not real-user failure patterns.
Workbooks: interactive reports that combine queries, metrics, and parameters. Use them for custom dashboards or SLA reports; they do not detect anomalies or send notifications themselves.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank creates a log search alert rule that fires when a loan-processing agent records more than 20 failed tool calls in five minutes. When the alert fires, a predefined remediation script that restarts the tool backend must run automatically, without human intervention.

What should you attach to the alert rule?
choices: A diagnostic setting that sends logs to a Log Analytics workspace
An action group that contains an Automation Runbook action
An Azure Monitor workbook that visualizes failed tool calls
An action group that contains an email and SMS notification action
explanation: Azure Monitor separates detection from response: the alert rule detects the condition, and its action groups define what happens next. Notification actions (email, SMS, push) inform people, while automation actions (Automation runbook, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, webhook) remediate automatically.
rationale: Incorrect: a diagnostic setting routes platform logs and metrics of a resource to a destination such as a Log Analytics workspace. It feeds data to an alert but cannot react when the alert fires. Use it when the log data is not yet collected.

Correct: an alert rule calls its action groups, and an action group can contain an Automation Runbook action that starts a predefined runbook. The restart runs as soon as the alert fires, with no person involved.

Incorrect: a workbook is an interactive report that can chart the failed tool calls, which helps triage but performs no action. Use a workbook when the team needs a shared view of trends, not automated remediation.

Incorrect: email and SMS actions notify people, who must then restart the backend themselves, which violates the no-human-intervention requirement. Use these actions when an on-call engineer must decide on the fix.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. has a claims-triage agent named Agent1. Production traffic changes every week, so the team wants to detect behavioral drift by comparing Agent1 against the same fixed set of reference questions and expected answers every day at 06:00. The results must appear on the Monitor tab of the agent.

What should you configure?
choices: A scheduled evaluation that uses a golden dataset as the data source
A scheduled red team scan that uses an evaluation template
A continuous evaluation that uses live traffic with random sampling
A continuous evaluation that uses live traffic with intelligent sampling
explanation: Drift detection needs a stable baseline: run the same golden dataset on a schedule so that score changes can be attributed to the agent itself. Continuous evaluation complements it by scoring live traffic for quality regressions, and red team scans cover safety.
rationale: Correct: a scheduled evaluation runs at a fixed time, and a golden dataset supplies the same questions and expected answers every day. Because the input never changes, a score change reflects drift in the agent, and the results appear on the Monitor tab.

Incorrect: a scheduled red team scan probes the agent with adversarial prompts to find safety risks. It does not compare answers with expected reference answers. Use it for recurring safety testing, not for drift against a baseline.

Incorrect: continuous evaluation scores sampled live traffic. Traffic changes every week, so score changes mix traffic shifts with behavior changes, and the rule has no fixed 06:00 run. Use it to watch quality on real production requests.

Incorrect: intelligent sampling selects more informative live requests, but the input is still changing production traffic and the rule runs continuously, not daily at 06:00. Use it when you evaluate live traffic and want better coverage per sample.

stem:
Northwind Traders builds an order-fulfilment workflow by using Microsoft Agent Framework workflows in Python. Instrumentation is enabled and traces are exported to Application Insights. Some orders stall because an executor never receives the message sent by the previous executor. You suspect that the target executor cannot handle the message type.

Which span attribute should you query to confirm the cause?
choices: gen_ai.operation.name
gen_ai.tool.call.result
edge_group.delivery_status
code.function.return.value
explanation: Workflow observability in Agent Framework adds spans for executor processing and for edge routing between executors. When messages stall, inspect the edge spans: the delivery status shows whether a message was delivered or dropped, for example because of a type mismatch.
rationale: Incorrect: gen_ai.operation.name names the generative AI operation of a span, such as chat or invoke_agent. It tells you what kind of call happened, not whether a workflow message reached its target executor. Use it to filter spans by operation type.

Incorrect: gen_ai.tool.call.result stores the result that a tool returned to the model. Messages between workflow executors are not tool calls, so this attribute says nothing about routing. Use it when you debug tool output.

Correct: Agent Framework workflows emit edge_group.process spans whose edge_group.delivery_status attribute records the routing outcome. A value of dropped type mismatch confirms that the target executor cannot handle the message type.

Incorrect: code.function.return.value is recorded by the @trace_function decorator for custom functions. It shows what a function returned, not how a message was routed between executors. Use it when you trace your own helper functions.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles runs a LangGraph agent on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS). The company wants to track the error rate of the agent and run continuous evaluations from Microsoft Foundry, next to the agents that run in Foundry Agent Service. The LangGraph agent already emits traces that follow the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for generative AI.

What should you do?
choices: Add the llm-emit-token-metric policy to the API Management API that fronts the agent
Register the agent in Foundry Control Plane and send its telemetry to the Application Insights resource of the project
Create a separate Application Insights resource for the agent and add it to an Azure Monitor workbook
Create Resource Health alerts for the AKS cluster that hosts the LangGraph agent
explanation: Foundry can monitor agents that run elsewhere when two conditions hold: the agent is registered in Foundry Control Plane, and its GenAI-convention telemetry lands in the Application Insights resource connected to the project. The same dashboard and continuous evaluation then apply to agents on any host.
rationale: Incorrect: llm-emit-token-metric sends token counts from API Management to Application Insights. It measures consumption at the gateway but does not register the agent in Foundry or enable Foundry evaluations. Use it for token reporting per consumer.

Correct: registering the LangGraph agent in Foundry Control Plane and sending its OpenTelemetry data to the project's Application Insights resource lets Foundry show its error rate and run continuous evaluations next to the hosted agents.

Incorrect: a separate Application Insights resource keeps the telemetry outside the resource connected to the project, so Foundry cannot monitor or evaluate the agent. A workbook only charts the data. Use this when the agent must stay outside Foundry.

Incorrect: Resource Health reports whether the AKS cluster is Available or Degraded on the platform. It provides no agent error rate and no quality evaluation. Use it to detect platform problems with the cluster.

stem:
Litware, Inc. exposes a customer service agent through a web API that is instrumented with Application Insights. The failure rate of requests rises and falls with load, so the team cannot choose a fixed alert threshold. The team needs near real-time notification when the failure rate rises abnormally compared to the previous days, including an analysis of the characteristics of the failures. The team does not want to write or configure alert logic.

Which feature should you use?
choices: Smart detection of failure anomalies
A metric alert rule with a static failed-requests threshold
An Application Insights standard availability test
A log search alert rule that runs a KQL query every five minutes
explanation: Azure Monitor alert rules (metric and log search) require you to define the signal and threshold, while Application Insights smart detection needs no setup and detects failure anomalies against learned history. Choose smart detection when the baseline varies and you want analysis without writing rules.
rationale: Correct: smart detection learns the normal failure rate of the app and alerts in near real time when it rises abnormally compared with earlier days. The notification includes an analysis of failure characteristics, and no alert logic has to be written.

Incorrect: a metric alert with a static threshold fires when failed requests cross a fixed value. The failure rate varies with load, so any fixed value is either noisy or late. Use it when the normal value is stable.

Incorrect: a Standard availability test sends synthetic requests to an endpoint and reports reachability. It does not analyze the failure rate of real user requests. Use it to detect outages of a public endpoint.

Incorrect: a log search alert runs a KQL query that you write against a threshold that you choose, which conflicts with the no-configuration requirement, and it adds no failure analysis. Use it when you need custom conditions over log data.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. configured a continuous evaluation rule for a high-traffic support agent by using the Python SDK. The project managed identity has the Foundry User role. Evaluation scores appear on the Monitor tab during most of the day, but the charts show gaps during peak business hours, and the evaluation runs list shows that runs are skipped during those hours.

What should you do to remove the gaps?
choices: Assign the Foundry User role to the project managed identity at the subscription scope
Replace the continuous evaluation rule with a daily scheduled evaluation
Increase the max_hourly_runs value of the evaluation rule
Expand the time range of the Monitor tab and refresh the dashboard
explanation: Continuous evaluation rules sample live traffic within an hourly budget set by max_hourly_runs. When peaks exceed the budget, runs are skipped and charts show gaps; raise the limit and accept the higher evaluation cost. Distinguish skipped runs (limits) from failed runs (permissions) and empty charts (ingestion delay).
rationale: Incorrect: Foundry User at subscription scope broadens access but changes nothing here, because evaluations already succeed outside peak hours with the current role. A permission problem would fail every run. Fix roles when all runs fail with authorization errors.

Incorrect: a daily scheduled evaluation runs once on a fixed dataset, so it stops scoring live peak traffic and misses regressions there. Use scheduled evaluation for drift against a golden dataset, not as a replacement for continuous evaluation.

Correct: skipped runs that cluster in peak hours mean the rule reached its hourly run cap. Raising max_hourly_runs above the default of 100 lets the rule evaluate more samples per hour, which removes the gaps.

Incorrect: a wider time range helps when charts are empty because data is still being ingested. Here the runs list shows runs as skipped, so results were never produced. Widen the range when results are delayed, not skipped.

stem:
Fourth Coffee needs automated remediation for an ordering agent. When more than 20 failed tool calls are recorded in an Application Insights resource named AppInsights1 within five minutes, an Azure Automation runbook must restart the backend that hosts the tools, without human intervention. You have an Automation account that has a user-assigned managed identity, and the remediation script is ready.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: Create and publish the runbook in the Automation account.
Create an action group named AG1 that has an Automation Runbook action that references the published runbook.

Run `az monitor scheduled-query create --name ToolFailures --resource-group RG1 --scopes <AppInsights1-id> --condition "count 'rows' > 20" --condition-query rows=@tool-failures.kql --window-size 5m --evaluation-frequency 5m --action-groups <AG1-id>`.
Create an action group named AG1 that has an email action and an SMS action for the on-call engineer.
Run `az monitor activity-log alert create --name ToolFailures --resource-group RG1 --condition category=ServiceHealth --action-group <AG1-id>`.
explanation: Automated remediation chains three objects that each reference the previous one: the runbook, the action group that starts it, and the alert rule that calls the action group. Create them in dependency order. Log search alerts (scheduled-query) evaluate KQL over your telemetry, while activity log alerts react to platform events.
rationale: Step 1: the Automation Runbook action of an action group lets you select only an existing runbook, so the runbook must be created and published first. Publishing makes the runbook available to be started by the alert.
Step 2: the action group links the alert to the remediation. Its Automation Runbook action references the published runbook and starts it automatically, so no person has to act when the alert fires.

Step 3: az monitor scheduled-query create builds the log search alert over the AppInsights1 data with a five-minute window. --action-groups needs the ID of AG1, so the action group must already exist.

Incorrect: an action group with email and SMS actions only notifies the on-call engineer, who then restarts the backend by hand, which breaks the no-human-intervention requirement. Use it when a person must approve the fix.

Incorrect: an activity log alert on the ServiceHealth category fires on published Azure platform incidents, not on failed tool calls in your telemetry. Use it to learn about regional service issues that affect your resources.

stem:
You need to meet the quality monitoring requirement for the booking agent.

What should you add to the monitoring strategy?
choices: Continuous evaluation with agent evaluators such as task adherence and intent resolution
An alert rule on token usage for the agent
An Application Insights Standard availability test for the agent endpoint
An alert rule on run success rate with a threshold of 99.5 percent
explanation: Operational metrics (run success rate, latency, token usage) show whether an agent runs, not whether it answers correctly. Quality regressions need evaluators: agent evaluators such as task adherence and intent resolution, run continuously on sampled production traffic, catch wrong outcomes that technical metrics miss.
rationale: Correct: task adherence and intent resolution evaluators judge whether the agent did what the user asked. Run as continuous evaluation on live traffic, they flag bookings with wrong dates automatically, even while run success rate and latency look healthy.

Incorrect: an alert on token usage reacts to how many tokens runs consume, which helps control cost. Correct and wrongly dated bookings use similar token counts, so the alert stays silent. Use it when cost spikes are the concern.
Incorrect: a Standard availability test checks that a public endpoint answers from several locations. The agent is reachable and fast, so the test passes. Use it to detect outages, not wrong answers.

Incorrect: the dashboard already shows a 99 percent run success rate because the runs complete technically. A stricter threshold still sees no failures, since the problem is answer quality. Tighten it when technical failures are the risk.

stem:
A. Datum Corporation runs an orchestrator agent that invokes three remote subagents over HTTP. Each subagent calls tools. All components export OpenTelemetry data to one Application Insights resource, but in the Foundry portal each subagent invocation appears as a separate, unrelated trace. You need a single trace tree that shows the orchestrator, each subagent invocation, and each tool execution.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Enable baggage propagation so that user identifiers flow to each subagent
Enable content recording for message contents in each subagent
Record each subagent invocation as an invoke_agent child span and each tool call as an execute_tool child span
Propagate W3C Trace Context headers, such as traceparent, on calls from the orchestrator to the subagents
Set a unique OTEL_SERVICE_NAME for each subagent so that each appears as its own cloud role
explanation: A single trace tree across services needs propagation and structure. Propagation (traceparent) keeps one trace ID across process boundaries, and structure (invoke_agent and execute_tool child spans) gives each step its place in the tree. Service names and content recording improve analysis but do not correlate spans.
rationale: Incorrect: baggage carries key-value pairs such as user identifiers next to the trace context, and it can leak PII. It does not replace traceparent, so subagent spans still start new traces. Use baggage only for non-sensitive context that downstream services need.

Incorrect: content recording adds prompts, responses, and tool arguments to spans. Each span gets richer, but nothing links spans across the HTTP boundary. Enable it in development when you need to see message content.

Correct: the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions model each subagent invocation as an invoke_agent span and each tool call as an execute_tool span, nested under the caller. That nesting produces the orchestrator, subagent, and tool hierarchy.

Correct: W3C Trace Context headers such as traceparent carry the trace ID and parent span ID over HTTP. Without them, each remote subagent starts a new, unrelated trace, which is exactly the symptom in the stem.

Incorrect: a unique OTEL_SERVICE_NAME per subagent sets cloud_RoleName, which separates components in queries and Application map. It does not join spans into one trace. Use it to tell components apart in a shared resource.

stem:
Litware, Inc. exposes a multi-agent solution through a public HTTPS endpoint. The operations team needs synthetic checks that send a request to the endpoint every five minutes from several Azure regions and validate the response code and the TLS certificate.

Which monitoring feature should the team use?
choices: A Service Health alert
An Application Insights Standard test
A Resource Health alert
The Application Insights application map
explanation: Synthetic monitoring tests your endpoint from outside on a schedule, independent of user traffic. Standard tests are the current Application Insights option and validate status codes, content, and TLS certificates from multiple locations. Platform signals such as Service Health and Resource Health complement them but do not test your endpoint.
rationale: Incorrect: a Service Health alert notifies you about published Azure incidents, planned maintenance, and advisories for a service and region. It does not probe your own endpoint. Use it to learn about platform problems that may affect you.

Correct: an Application Insights Standard test sends a request to a public URL at a set frequency, such as every five minutes, from several locations, and validates the response code and the TLS certificate, which covers each requirement.

Incorrect: a Resource Health alert reports health changes of an Azure resource as detected by the platform, such as Unavailable or Degraded. It sends no synthetic requests and checks no certificate. Use it for platform-detected resource problems.

Incorrect: Application map visualizes components and calls from real telemetry. It shows nothing when no users call the endpoint and does not validate TLS. Use it to locate failing components in a distributed application.

stem:
Coho Winery streams responses from chat agents that use an Azure OpenAI model on a provisioned deployment. The operations team defines three monitoring needs.

Which metric should the team use for each need? To answer, drag the appropriate metrics to the correct needs. Each metric may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
choices: Time to Response
Time Between Tokens
Time to Last Byte
Provisioned-managed Utilization V2
Processed Prompt Tokens
targets: Need1: how quickly users see the first part of each streamed response after they send a prompt
Need2: how fast the model generates tokens once a streamed response has started
Need3: how close the deployment is to the capacity at which new calls return HTTP 429
explanation: Azure OpenAI exposes separate latency metrics for each phase: Time to Response for the first output, Time Between Tokens for generation speed, and Time to Last Byte for the full response. Capacity of provisioned deployments is tracked with Provisioned-managed Utilization V2. Do not use the legacy Cognitive Services Latency metric for Azure OpenAI.
rationale: Need1 is first-token responsiveness for streaming. Time to Response measures the time from the prompt until the first response arrives, which is the recommended responsiveness metric for streaming requests.
Need2 is generation speed after the first token. Time Between Tokens measures the interval between generated tokens, so it isolates decoding speed from queueing and prompt processing.
Need3 is capacity headroom on a provisioned deployment. Provisioned-managed Utilization V2 reports PTUs consumed divided by PTUs deployed, and calls are throttled with 429 at 100 percent.
notes: Time to Response: time until the first response of a request. Use it for perceived responsiveness of streaming chats. It is not available for Standard deployments.
Time Between Tokens: the interval between generated tokens. Use it to monitor generation speed once output has started, for example after a model or load change.
Time to Last Byte: time until the full response is received. Use it for overall response time, and pair it with token counts to tell expected from unexpected changes.
Provisioned-managed Utilization V2: the percentage of provisioned capacity in use. Use it to alert before a PTU deployment reaches 100 percent and starts returning 429 responses.
Processed Prompt Tokens: the number of input tokens processed. Use it to track prompt size and input cost trends, and as a companion to latency metrics, not as a latency or capacity metric.

stem:
Humongous Insurance needs the on-call engineer to receive an email when the Foundry resource named Foundry1 in resource group RG1 becomes Unavailable or Degraded, even when no broader Azure platform incident is published for the region. Foundry1 is in a subscription named Sub1, but your Azure CLI session currently uses a different default subscription.

Which three commands should you run in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate commands from the list of commands to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `az account set --subscription Sub1`
`az monitor action-group create --name AG1 --resource-group RG1 --short-name AG1 --action email oncall <oncall-email>`
`az monitor activity-log alert create --name Foundry1Health --resource-group RG1 --scope <Foundry1-id> --condition category=ResourceHealth --action-group <AG1-id>`
`az monitor activity-log alert create --name Foundry1Health --resource-group RG1 --scope <Foundry1-id> --condition category=ServiceHealth --action-group <AG1-id>`
`az monitor metrics alert create --name Foundry1Idle --resource-group RG1 --scopes <Foundry1-id> --condition "total ProcessedPromptTokens < 1" --action <AG1-id>`
explanation: Resource Health and Service Health events both arrive in the activity log and are distinguished by category: ResourceHealth covers the health of your individual resources, ServiceHealth covers published service-wide incidents. Both use activity log alerts that call action groups, so create the action group first and pass its ID to the alert.
rationale: Step 1: az account set switches the CLI context to Sub1. Later commands create resources in the active subscription, so it must run first, or the action group and the alert land in the wrong subscription.

Step 2: az monitor action-group create defines who is notified, here an email action for the on-call engineer. The alert rule in the next step references the ID of this action group, so it must exist first.

Step 3: an activity log alert on category=ResourceHealth fires when the platform reports a health change of a resource, including Unavailable and Degraded, even when no regional incident is published. --scope limits the rule to events of Foundry1; without it, the rule covers the whole subscription.

Incorrect: category=ServiceHealth fires on published Azure service incidents and maintenance for a region. The requirement asks for an alert even when no such incident exists. Use it to follow broad platform issues.
Incorrect: a metric alert on zero processed prompt tokens also fires in quiet periods and does not reflect the health status of the resource. Use token metrics to monitor usage, not availability.

stem:
Blue Yonder Airlines runs its flight-status agents on a Global Provisioned deployment in a Foundry resource named Foundry1. The team needs an email alert when the deployment approaches full capacity so that it can act before requests are throttled. You script the setup in the Azure CLI, and the alert command must receive the action group resource ID from a lookup command.

Which three commands should you run in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate commands from the list of commands to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `az monitor action-group create --name AG1 --resource-group RG1 --short-name AG1 --action email OnCall <oncall-email>`
`az monitor action-group show --name AG1 --resource-group RG1 --query id -o tsv`
`az monitor metrics alert create --name PtuHigh --resource-group RG1 --scopes <Foundry1-id> --condition "avg AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilizationV2 > 90" --action <AG1-id>`
`az monitor metrics alert create --name PtuHigh --resource-group RG1 --scopes <Foundry1-id> --condition "avg AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilization > 90" --action <AG1-id>`
`az monitor activity-log alert create --name PtuHigh --resource-group RG1 --condition category=ResourceHealth --action-group <AG1-id>`
explanation: Provisioned capacity is measured as PTUs consumed divided by PTUs deployed and exposed as Provisioned-managed Utilization V2 (AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilizationV2). Alert below 100 percent to act before 429 responses start, and create the action group, look up its ID, and then create the metric alert, because each step needs the output of the previous one.
rationale: Step 1: az monitor action-group create builds AG1 with an email action named OnCall for the on-call engineer. The action group must exist before its ID can be looked up or referenced by an alert rule.

Step 2: az monitor action-group show with --query id -o tsv returns only the resource ID of AG1 as plain text. The script passes this value to --action of the metric alert in the next step, so the lookup runs after creation and before the alert.

Step 3: the metric alert watches AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilizationV2, the recommended PTU utilization metric. A threshold of 90 percent warns before utilization reaches 100 percent, where new calls return 429.

Incorrect: AzureOpenAIProvisionedManagedUtilization is the original utilization metric, which is deprecated and replaced by the V2 metric. You meet it only in older charts or alert rules that still reference it.

Incorrect: a Resource Health activity log alert fires when the platform marks Foundry1 as Unavailable or Degraded. A fully utilized deployment is healthy, so this alert stays silent. Use it to detect platform outages of the resource.

stem:
Wide World Importers sees the average Time to Last Byte of its Azure OpenAI deployment increase by 40 percent over one week. The team must decide whether this indicates a real service problem or expected behavior caused by the agents producing longer answers.

Which metric should the team chart next to Time to Last Byte?
choices: Blocked Volume
Prompt Token Cache Match Rate
Potential Abusive User Count
Generated Completion Tokens
explanation: Read latency metrics together with token metrics, because longer outputs take longer to generate. Microsoft recommends pairing every latency metric with a token count metric: a latency rise without a token rise points to a service issue, while a proportional rise is expected behavior.
rationale: Incorrect: Blocked Volume counts requests that content filtering blocked. It is a Content Safety metric and does not explain why the time to the last byte grows. Use it when you investigate filter behavior or abuse.

Incorrect: Prompt Token Cache Match Rate shows how many prompt tokens hit the prompt cache, which affects input processing. It does not show whether answers got longer. Use it when you tune prompts for caching.

Incorrect: Potential Abusive User Count is a Content Safety metric that estimates users with abusive patterns. It has no link to output length or latency. Use it for abuse monitoring together with Blocked Volume.

Correct: Time to Last Byte grows with the number of generated tokens. If Generated Completion Tokens rose by a similar proportion, the latency change is expected; if it did not, there may be a real service problem.

stem:
Trey Research hosts its agent API in an Azure Container Apps environment. The API is reachable only through a private endpoint, and inbound traffic from the internet is blocked by policy. A Container Apps job inside the same virtual network calls the API health endpoint every minute and writes each failed probe to its console log. The logs destination of the environment is set to Azure Monitor, but no diagnostic setting exists. You need an alert that calls the existing action group AG1 when probes fail. No Log Analytics workspace exists yet.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `az monitor log-analytics workspace create --resource-group RG1 --workspace-name WS1 --location eastus --query id -o tsv`
`az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name ToWS1 --resource <environment-id> --workspace <WS1-id> --logs '[{"categoryGroup":"allLogs","enabled":true}]'`
`az monitor scheduled-query create --name ProbeFailed --resource-group RG1 --scopes <WS1-id> --condition "count 'rows' > 0" --condition-query rows=@probe-failures.kql --action-groups <AG1-id>`
Create an Application Insights Standard test that calls the API URL from five public test locations every five minutes.
`az monitor activity-log alert create --name AcaHealth --resource-group RG1 --condition category=ServiceHealth --action-group <AG1-id>`
explanation: For endpoints without public ingress, synthetic tests from Azure test locations cannot connect. Microsoft recommends an internal health signal from inside the network instead: collect it into Log Analytics, for example through a diagnostic setting, and alert on it with a log or metric alert.
rationale: Step 1: the workspace is both the destination of the logs and the scope of the alert. The two later commands need its resource ID, so it must be created first.

Step 2: the diagnostic setting on the Container Apps environment sends all log categories, including the console output of the probe job, to WS1. Without it, the workspace holds no probe data for the alert query.
Step 3: the log search alert runs probe-failures.kql against WS1 and calls AG1 when the query returns rows. It depends on the workspace ID and on the probe logs that the diagnostic setting delivers.

Incorrect: Standard tests run from public Azure test locations and need an endpoint that is reachable from the internet. The private endpoint blocks them, so the test would always fail. Use Standard tests for public endpoints.

Incorrect: a Service Health alert fires on published Azure incidents for Container Apps in the region. It does not fire when your own API stops responding. Use it to stay informed about platform-wide issues.

stem:
You need to meet the availability requirement for the Azure OpenAI endpoint that the agents use.

What should you recommend?
choices: Deploy resources in two regions behind an API Management backend pool that has circuit breaker rules
Configure spillover from the primary deployment to a standard deployment in the same resource
Request a quota increase for the deployment in the primary region
Add retry logic that honors the retry-after-ms header in each agent
explanation: Business continuity for Standard deployments relies on redundant resources in more than one region plus a generative AI gateway, such as API Management, that load balances and opens a circuit breaker when one backend fails. Consumers see one endpoint, so failover needs no code change.
rationale: Correct: Foundry resources in two EU regions behind an API Management backend pool with load balancing and circuit breaker rules let the gateway route around a regional outage. The agents keep calling the same gateway, so no agent code changes.

Incorrect: spillover moves overflow traffic from a provisioned deployment to a standard deployment in the same resource. Foundry1 uses Data Zone Standard, and same-resource routing does not survive a regional outage. Use spillover to absorb PTU peaks.

Incorrect: more quota in West Europe raises the rate limit in that region only. During a regional outage, the endpoint is unreachable whatever the quota. Request more quota when 429 responses, not outages, are the problem.

Incorrect: retry logic that honors retry-after-ms helps with transient throttling, but the case forbids agent code changes for availability, and retries against an unreachable region keep failing. Add retries in code you control for 429 handling.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute creates an Application Insights Standard test for its tutoring agent endpoint. The test runs from five test locations every five minutes, retries for test failures are enabled, and the alert location threshold is set to 3.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: The alert location threshold follows the recommended relationship for five test locations.
A location reports a failure only after three successive attempts from that location fail.
The test can target the private endpoint IP address of the API, which is reachable only from the company virtual network.
explanation: Standard tests reduce false alerts in two layers: retries filter transient failures at each location, and the alert location threshold (number of locations minus 2) filters problems that affect only one or two locations. They can test only endpoints that are reachable from the internet.
rationale: Yes: Microsoft recommends an alert location threshold equal to the number of test locations minus 2, with at least five locations. Five minus two is three, which filters single-location noise but still alerts on real outages.

Yes: with retries enabled, a failed test retries after a short interval and reports a failure only if three successive attempts fail. The rule applies independently at each location, and most transient failures disappear on retry.

No: the URL of a Standard test must be visible from the public internet, because requests come from Azure test locations. For a private endpoint, monitor an internal health signal from inside the network and alert on it instead.

stem:
Alpine Ski House runs a booking agent on a Global Provisioned deployment of gpt-4.1 in a Foundry resource named Foundry1. During weekend peaks, the deployment returns HTTP 429 responses because utilization reaches 100 percent. The company must process the overflow requests instead of failing them, keep the provisioned deployment as the primary target, and avoid changing the agent code. Foundry1 contains a Global Standard deployment of the same model version. A second resource named Foundry2 in another region also contains a Global Standard deployment of that model version.

What should you do?
choices: Set spilloverDeploymentName on the provisioned deployment to the Global Standard deployment in Foundry1
Set spilloverDeploymentName on the provisioned deployment to the Global Standard deployment in Foundry2
Increase max_retries on the OpenAI client so that throttled agent requests are retried later
Add the x-ms-spillover-deployment header with the Foundry1 deployment name to each agent request
explanation: Spillover keeps a provisioned deployment as the primary target and sends requests that would receive 429 to a standard deployment in the same resource. Enable it for all traffic with the deployment property spilloverDeploymentName, or per request with the x-ms-spillover-deployment header.
rationale: Correct: spilloverDeploymentName is a property of the provisioned deployment. Pointing it at the Global Standard deployment in Foundry1 sends overflow to standard capacity while the PTU deployment stays primary, with no agent code change.

Incorrect: a spillover target must be a standard deployment in the same Foundry resource as the provisioned deployment. Foundry2 is a different resource in another region, so it cannot be the target. Use a gateway such as API Management to route across resources.

Incorrect: max_retries makes the client wait and retry after a 429, which adds latency and still depends on free PTU capacity. It is also a code change. Use retries when longer latency is acceptable and spillover is not available.

Incorrect: the x-ms-spillover-deployment header enables spillover per request, so every agent request must be changed to send it, which breaks the no-code-change requirement. Use the header when only some requests may spill over.

stem:
VanArsdel, Ltd. runs agents on a Standard deployment that has 300,000 TPM assigned. During a sustained burst, the agents receive HTTP 429 responses. Azure Monitor shows billed token usage at about half of the assigned TPM, requests are spread evenly over each minute, and max_tokens is sized to the expected answers. The x-ratelimit-limit-tokens response header reports a value lower than 300,000.

What should you do first?
choices: Increase the TPM allocated to the deployment from the unused subscription quota
Retry the throttled requests by honoring the retry-after-ms header
Submit a quota increase request for the model in the region
Reduce the max_tokens value in each request
explanation: Standard deployments share capacity, and the effective limit can temporarily drop below the configured TPM. Check the x-ratelimit-limit-tokens header: when it is lower than your assignment, handle 429 responses with retry-after-ms backoff, and consider provisioned throughput if the problem persists.
rationale: Incorrect: allocating more TPM raises the configured limit, but the header already shows an effective limit below the configured 300,000 TPM because the shared pool lowered it temporarily. Allocate more TPM when usage really reaches the configured limit.

Correct: an x-ratelimit-limit-tokens value below the assigned TPM, with burst patterns and max_tokens ruled out, indicates a temporary rate limit adjustment of the shared Standard pool. The first response is to retry with retry-after-ms backoff.

Incorrect: a quota increase raises how much TPM you can assign in the region. The assigned TPM is not the bottleneck, because billed usage is about half of it. Request quota when deployments cannot get the TPM they need.

Incorrect: max_tokens counts toward rate limit estimation, but it is already sized to the expected answers. Lowering it further would truncate answers without changing the lowered effective limit. Reduce it when it is set far above real answer length.

stem:
Southridge Video must report monthly whether Azure met its service-level agreement (SLA) for the Foundry resource that hosts its agents. The on-call engineer must also be notified when the resource becomes unavailable because of an Azure platform event rather than an action by the team.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Review the activity log of the Foundry resource
Create a Resource Health alert that filters on the User initiated reason type
Create a Resource Health alert that filters on the Platform initiated reason type
Create a Service Health alert for service issues in the region
Review the Resource Health history of the Foundry resource
explanation: Resource Health is the per-resource availability signal: its history supports SLA verification, and its alerts can be filtered by reason type to separate platform-initiated from user-initiated events. Service Health and the activity log answer other questions: published incidents and change audit.
rationale: Incorrect: the activity log records control-plane operations on the resource, such as configuration changes and who made them. It does not record availability history, so it cannot prove SLA compliance. Use it to audit changes.

Incorrect: the User initiated reason type matches health events caused by your own actions, such as stopping or reconfiguring the resource. The requirement covers platform events only. Use it to track downtime that the team caused.

Correct: a Resource Health alert filtered on the Platform initiated reason type fires only when Azure, not the team, makes the resource unavailable, so the on-call engineer is notified about platform events only.

Incorrect: a Service Health alert covers broad, published incidents for a service and region. A single resource can become unavailable without such an incident, so this alert can miss it. Use it for region-wide awareness.

Correct: Resource Health history shows the current and past health of the Foundry resource, including periods when it was unavailable because of Azure problems, which is the evidence needed for a monthly SLA report.

stem:
Wingtip Toys runs a latency-critical pricing agent on a Global Standard deployment. Traffic is high and sustained. During business hours, response latency becomes more than two times higher than at night, and occasional HTTP 429 responses occur. The business requires consistent, predictable latency at scale.

What should you recommend?
choices: Implement retry logic with exponential backoff in the pricing agent
Submit a quota increase request for the Global Standard deployment
Move the workload to a provisioned throughput (PTU) deployment
Switch to a Data Zone Standard deployment
explanation: Standard deployment types (Global, Data Zone, and regional) share capacity, so latency varies with load. Provisioned throughput (PTU) reserves capacity and is recommended for latency-critical or high, sustained workloads; quota increases and retries only address throttling.
rationale: Incorrect: exponential backoff absorbs 429 responses, but each retry adds waiting time, so latency becomes higher and less predictable. Use retries when occasional delays are acceptable, not when latency must stay consistent.

Incorrect: more Global Standard quota reduces 429 responses, but the capacity is still shared, so latency still varies with demand during business hours. Request quota when throttling, not latency consistency, is the issue.

Correct: provisioned throughput reserves dedicated capacity for the deployment, which gives consistent, predictable latency at scale and removes the shared-pool variability that doubles latency during peak hours.

Incorrect: Data Zone Standard keeps processing within a data zone, which addresses data residency. It is still shared, pay-per-token capacity, so latency under sustained load behaves like Global Standard. Use it when data must stay in a geography.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. builds a research agent by using Microsoft Agent Framework in Python. When the model keeps requesting tools, a single request can trigger many model round trips. You need to limit the number of model and tool round trips that the chat client performs for each request.

Which function invocation setting should you configure?
choices: allow_concurrent_invocation
max_function_calls
max_duration_seconds
max_iterations
explanation: FunctionInvocationConfiguration bounds the automatic tool loop in several ways: max_iterations for model round trips, max_function_calls for total tool executions, max_duration_seconds for elapsed time, and max_consecutive_errors_per_request for repeated failures. Pick the control that matches the budget you must enforce.
rationale: Incorrect: allow_concurrent_invocation controls whether function calls from one model response run in parallel. It changes speed, not the number of model round trips per request. Set it to False when tools share state or must run in model order.

Incorrect: max_function_calls caps the total number of tool executions per request, not model round trips. One round trip can contain several tool calls, so it measures something else. Use it when the requirement is a tool-call budget.
Incorrect: max_duration_seconds stops tool invocation after a wall-clock limit, regardless of how many round trips occurred. Use it when the requirement is a time budget per request.
Correct: max_iterations limits how many times the client sends function results back to the model in a new request, which is the number of model and tool round trips per request. The default is 40.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. calls a reasoning model through the Azure OpenAI Responses API. You need to cap the total number of tokens that the model generates for each request, including reasoning tokens and visible output tokens.

Which parameter should you set?
choices: max_completion_tokens
max_output_tokens
reasoning.context
reasoning.effort
explanation: Reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens and count toward the output limit. Cap them with max_output_tokens in the Responses API or max_completion_tokens in Chat Completions; reasoning.effort only influences how many tokens the model tends to spend.
rationale: Incorrect: max_completion_tokens is the Chat Completions API parameter that caps reasoning plus visible output tokens. The stem uses the Responses API, which has its own parameter. Use max_completion_tokens with Chat Completions requests.

Correct: in the Responses API, max_output_tokens caps all tokens that the model generates for the response, including reasoning tokens and visible output, so it bounds the billable output of each request.

Incorrect: reasoning.context controls which earlier reasoning is carried into the request, which affects context size, not a hard cap on generated tokens. Use it to decide whether reasoning from earlier turns is reused.
Incorrect: reasoning.effort sets how much the model reasons, such as low or high. Lower effort usually uses fewer tokens but sets no upper bound. Use it to trade answer depth for cost and latency.

stem:
Tailspin Toys has a Foundry toolbox that contains 35 tools shared by several agents. Token costs grow with each tool that is added because every tool definition is passed to the model on each turn.

What should you enable to keep token costs flat as the toolbox grows?
choices: Tool search in the toolbox
Concurrent tool invocation
Content recording for tool call arguments
A lower max_iterations value
explanation: Tool definitions are input tokens on every turn, so large tool catalogs make every request expensive. Tool search defers definitions and loads them only when the model needs them; Microsoft suggests it once a toolbox reaches roughly 10 to 15 tools.
rationale: Correct: tool search replaces the full list of tool definitions with meta-tools that let the model find and call tools on demand. Each turn carries a small fixed overhead, so token cost stays flat as the toolbox grows.

Incorrect: concurrent tool invocation runs several tool calls in parallel, which reduces wall-clock time. Every tool definition is still sent on each turn, so input tokens keep growing. Use it to speed up independent tool calls.

Incorrect: content recording adds tool arguments and messages to traces for debugging. It changes telemetry, not the prompt, so it does not reduce tokens. Enable it in development when you need to see tool inputs.
Incorrect: a lower max_iterations caps the number of round trips, but every remaining turn still carries all 35 definitions, so cost still grows with each added tool. Use it to bound runaway loops.

stem:
Relecloud builds a Python agent by using Microsoft Agent Framework. When a downstream service is unavailable, the tool that calls it fails, and the model keeps calling the tool again within the same request, which wastes tokens. You need automatic function calling to stop for the request after two consecutive tool errors.

Which function invocation setting should you configure?
choices: include_detailed_errors
terminate_on_unknown_calls
max_iterations
max_consecutive_errors_per_request
explanation: Loop controls react to different signals: consecutive errors (max_consecutive_errors_per_request), unknown tools (terminate_on_unknown_calls), and volume (max_iterations, max_function_calls). Choose the control that matches the failure mode you want to stop.
rationale: Incorrect: include_detailed_errors adds exception details to the function result that the model sees. It may help the model react, but it does not stop repeated calls. Enable it only on trusted channels, because exception text can contain sensitive data.

Incorrect: terminate_on_unknown_calls ends the loop when the model requests a tool that is not registered. Here the tool exists but fails, so the setting never triggers. Use it to stop on hallucinated tool names.

Incorrect: max_iterations caps round trips whether calls succeed or fail, so a failing tool can still consume the full limit, 40 by default. Use it as a general loop bound, not as an error-based stop.

Correct: max_consecutive_errors_per_request stops further function calls for the request after the set number of consecutive errors. A value of 2 stops wasting tokens on an unavailable service. The default is 3.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute calls a model through the Azure OpenAI Responses API with the file search and code interpreter built-in tools. For some requests, the model calls the built-in tools many times within one response, which increases token usage. You need to cap the total number of built-in tool calls per response at four, across both tools. The model must still decide on its own whether to use each tool.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",
    tools=builtin_tools,  # file_search and code_interpreter
    [[1]]=4,
    tool_choice=[[2]],
    input=question,
)
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Correct: max_tool_calls sets the maximum total number of built-in tool calls processed in one response, across all built-in tools, and further tool attempts are ignored, which caps the loop at four.

Incorrect: max_output_tokens caps generated tokens, and a value of 4 would cut the answer off almost immediately. It does not count tool calls. Use it to bound output and reasoning tokens per response.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Correct: auto lets the model decide on each step whether to call a tool, so both built-in tools remain available and the model chooses when to use them, as the requirement states.
Incorrect: required forces the model to call a tool even when a direct answer would do, which can add tool calls and tokens. Use it when every request must be grounded on a tool result.
Incorrect: none prevents the model from calling any tool, so file search and code interpreter can no longer be used. Use it when you want a plain text answer from a request that still lists tools.

explanation: The Responses API offers separate controls: max_tool_calls bounds built-in tool calls per response, tool_choice decides whether tools may or must be called, and max_output_tokens bounds generated tokens. Combine a call cap with tool_choice auto to limit cost without removing capabilities.

stem:
Northwind Traders configures a Microsoft Agent Framework chat client in Python. Each request must stop invoking tools after five model round trips, after 20 tool calls in total, or after 30 seconds, whichever comes first.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient()
client.function_invocation_configuration.update(
    {
        "max_iterations": 5,
        [[1]]: 20,
        [[2]]: 30.0,
    }
)
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Correct: max_function_calls caps the total number of tool executions per request. It defaults to None, which means unlimited, so setting it to 20 enforces the tool-call budget.

Incorrect: max_consecutive_errors_per_request stops after that many consecutive failed calls. Successful calls never count toward it, so 20 successful calls would not stop the loop. Use it to stop on repeated errors.

Incorrect: max_duration_seconds is the time budget. With 20 here, the client would stop after 20 seconds and the number of tool calls would stay unlimited. Use it for the wall-clock requirement instead.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Correct: max_duration_seconds stops tool invocation after the elapsed wall-clock time, here 30 seconds. Time spent waiting for tool approval also counts toward this limit.
Incorrect: max_function_calls would allow 30 tool calls instead of 30 seconds, and the key is already needed for the 20-call limit. Use it to count tool executions, not time.
Incorrect: max_iterations is already set to 5 for round trips; repeating the key would overwrite it with 30 and leave no time limit. Use it only for the round-trip requirement.

explanation: Agent Framework limits for automatic tool invocation are best effort and checked after each model-requested batch of tool calls, so a batch can overshoot. When any limit is reached, the client stops invoking tools and asks the model for a final text response.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing has five agents that share one Azure OpenAI deployment through Azure API Management. One agent occasionally enters a runaway state and sends many large prompts that consume most of the tokens-per-minute (TPM) capacity of the deployment, which throttles the other agents. Each agent sends a unique x-agent-id header. You need to cap token consumption per agent per minute so that a runaway agent receives HTTP 429 responses while the other agents continue to work.

Solution: You configure the rate-limit-by-key policy with a calls value and a counter-key based on the x-agent-id header.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: Call-based limits and token-based limits protect different things. Model capacity is measured in tokens, so a per-key token limit is required when large prompts are the risk.
rationale: Incorrect: rate-limit-by-key counts calls per key. A runaway agent that sends few but very large prompts stays under the call limit while it still consumes most of the TPM, so the other agents are still throttled.

Correct: the solution does not meet the goal. rate-limit-by-key is the right policy when you need to limit request rates per caller, for example to protect a backend from chatty clients, not token consumption.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing has five agents that share one Azure OpenAI deployment through Azure API Management. One agent occasionally enters a runaway state and sends many large prompts that consume most of the tokens-per-minute (TPM) capacity of the deployment, which throttles the other agents. Each agent sends a unique x-agent-id header. You need to cap token consumption per agent per minute so that a runaway agent receives HTTP 429 responses while the other agents continue to work.

Solution: You configure the llm-token-limit policy with a tokens-per-minute value and a counter-key based on the x-agent-id header.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: llm-token-limit enforces a token rate limit per counter key and returns 429 when it is exceeded. Keying the counter on a header that identifies the caller isolates a runaway agent from the others.
rationale: Correct: llm-token-limit counts tokens, not calls, per counter key. With tokens-per-minute and x-agent-id as the key, only the agent that exceeds its budget receives 429 Too Many Requests, while the others keep their own budgets.
Incorrect: the solution does meet the goal. No would be right if the policy counted calls instead of tokens, or if one shared counter key throttled all agents together.

stem:
Trey Research uses the following code to re-run a coding agent until its output contains the word DONE:

```python
from agent_framework import Agent, AgentLoopMiddleware

def needs_more_work(*, last_result, **kwargs):
    return "DONE" not in last_result.text

agent = Agent(
    client=client,
    middleware=[AgentLoopMiddleware(needs_more_work, max_iterations=5)],
)
```

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: If the model never writes DONE, the loop stops after five agent runs.
If max_iterations is removed from the code, the loop runs until the predicate returns False.
If an iteration returns a pending tool-approval request, the middleware returns the request to the caller before it evaluates needs_more_work.
explanation: Agent looping re-invokes an agent while a predicate returns True, and Microsoft advises always bounding autonomous loops because models can stall. AgentLoopMiddleware defaults to 10 runs and judge loops to five, while options such as fresh_context and inject_progress change the context, not the bound.
rationale: Yes: max_iterations=5 is a hard upper bound on agent runs. The predicate keeps returning True while DONE is missing, but the middleware stops at the bound, which caps token usage for tasks that never converge.

No: without the argument, AgentLoopMiddleware uses its default maximum of 10 agent runs, so the loop is still bounded. Only max_iterations=None removes the bound, which Microsoft advises only when the predicate is guaranteed to terminate.

Yes: the middleware stops before evaluating its continuation predicate when an iteration returns a pending tool-approval request, and it returns the request to the caller instead of hiding it behind another autonomous iteration.

stem:
Margie's Travel calls a reasoning model through the Responses API with max_output_tokens set to 2,000 for an itinerary-planning agent. For complex requests, some responses have status incomplete with incomplete_details.reason set to max_output_tokens and contain no visible output. The company is billed for these requests, and the agent shows them to users as empty answers. You need to reduce how often this occurs and prevent the agent from presenting incomplete responses as answers.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Set reasoning.context to all_turns so that earlier reasoning carries forward
Decrease max_output_tokens so that the model produces shorter reasoning
Set reasoning.effort to high for complex itinerary requests
Raise max_output_tokens to reserve enough room for reasoning and output
Check the status of each response and handle incomplete responses explicitly
explanation: A response can end incomplete because of max_output_tokens before any visible output exists, and you still pay for input and reasoning tokens. Reserve enough room for reasoning plus output, and always check the response status so that the application handles this case explicitly.
rationale: Incorrect: reasoning.context set to all_turns carries earlier reasoning forward, which adds context and tends to increase token use within the same 2,000-token limit. Use it when continuity of reasoning across turns matters more than cost.

Incorrect: a lower max_output_tokens leaves even less room for reasoning and visible output, so the limit is hit sooner and incomplete responses become more frequent. Lower it only when answers are reliably far below the limit.

Incorrect: high reasoning effort makes the model reason more, which consumes more reasoning tokens inside the same limit and raises the chance of an incomplete response. Use high effort when quality justifies more tokens and room is reserved.

Correct: reasoning tokens and visible output share max_output_tokens. Raising the limit reserves room for both, so complex itineraries can finish with a visible answer instead of stopping during reasoning.

Correct: checking status on every response lets the agent detect incomplete responses with reason max_output_tokens and handle them, for example by retrying with a larger limit, instead of showing an empty answer.

stem:
You need to meet the token budget requirement for the itinerary agent.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
choices: Declare the functions with defer_loading set to true and add the tool_search tool
Pass the reasoning items, function call items, and function call outputs from the previous response into the next request
Set allow_concurrent_invocation to False
Set reasoning.context to all_turns
Increase max_output_tokens
explanation: Two token sinks dominate tool-heavy reasoning agents: tool definitions sent on every request and reasoning that restarts after each function call. Tool search with deferred loading addresses the first, and passing reasoning items back between calls addresses the second.
rationale: Correct: functions declared with defer_loading set to true, together with the tool_search tool, are not sent in full on every request. The model loads definitions only when needed, which cuts input tokens for the 30 functions in the case.

Correct: passing reasoning items, function calls, and function outputs from the previous response into the next request, for example through previous_response_id, lets the model continue its reasoning instead of starting over, which saves tokens in function-call chains.

Incorrect: allow_concurrent_invocation is an Agent Framework setting that controls whether tool calls run in parallel. It affects execution order and speed, not the tokens sent to the model. Set it to False when tools must run in model order.
Incorrect: reasoning.context set to all_turns includes earlier reasoning in the context, which increases token consumption. Use it only when continuity across turns is worth the extra tokens.
Incorrect: a higher max_output_tokens allows the model to generate more tokens, so it can only raise consumption. Raise it when responses end incomplete, not to reduce cost.

stem:
Lucerne Publishing has five agents that share one Azure OpenAI deployment through Azure API Management. One agent occasionally enters a runaway state and sends many large prompts that consume most of the tokens-per-minute (TPM) capacity of the deployment, which throttles the other agents. Each agent sends a unique x-agent-id header. You need to cap token consumption per agent per minute so that a runaway agent receives HTTP 429 responses while the other agents continue to work.

Solution: You configure the llm-token-limit policy with a token-quota value, a token-quota-period of Hourly, and a counter-key based on the x-agent-id header.

Does this meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: llm-token-limit supports two modes: a tokens-per-minute rate limit that returns 429 and resets every minute, and a token-quota over a period from Hourly to Yearly that returns 403 until the quota resets. Choose the mode that matches the required time window and response.
rationale: Incorrect: a token quota counts tokens over the quota period and returns 403 Forbidden until the period resets. The goal requires a per-minute cap that returns 429, so an hourly quota blocks a runaway agent too long and with the wrong status code.
Correct: the solution does not meet the goal. token-quota with a period is the right choice for allowances, such as a monthly token budget per partner, not for per-minute rate limiting.

stem:
Litware, Inc. has four Foundry projects that share one Foundry resource and use Azure OpenAI models. The finance team needs to allocate the shared model spend to the business unit that owns each project, without adding tags manually.

What should the finance team do in Cost Management?
choices: Filter the cost analysis view by the project tag
Group the cost analysis view by Meter
Group the cost analysis view by Resource
Filter the cost analysis view by Service tier: Azure OpenAI
explanation: Chargeback needs a cost dimension that matches the owner. Foundry tags consumption with the project automatically, so projects on one shared resource can be charged back through a tag filter. Finer splits inside one project need gateway metrics, such as API Management token metrics.
rationale: Correct: Foundry adds a project tag to the consumption of each project, so filtering cost analysis on that tag splits the spend of the shared resource per project without manual tagging, for models sold by Azure.

Incorrect: grouping by Meter shows which priced units, such as input or output tokens of a model, drove cost. All projects use the same meters, so this does not split spend by project. Use it to see which models cost the most.
Incorrect: grouping by Resource shows cost per Azure resource. The four projects share one Foundry resource, so the result is one total. Use it when each business unit has its own resource.

Incorrect: a service filter for Azure OpenAI isolates model spend from other services, but it still returns one total for the shared resource. Use it to separate model cost from other services before you split by project.

stem:
Tailspin Toys must give three users read access for monitoring a Foundry solution. No user may receive permissions to manage resources.

Which role should you assign to each user? To answer, drag the appropriate roles to the correct users. Each role may be used once, more than once, or not at all.
choices: Cost Management Reader
Cognitive Services Usages Reader
Log Analytics Reader
Foundry User
Privileged Monitoring Data Reader
targets: User1: a financial analyst who views costs and usage charges for the Foundry resources in a resource group
User2: a capacity planner who views Azure OpenAI quota usage across the subscription
User3: an engineer who opens agent traces from the Application Insights resource connected to the project; the trace tables are not protected
explanation: Monitoring access is split by data type: costs (Cost Management Reader), quota (Cognitive Services Usages Reader), telemetry (Log Analytics Reader, plus Privileged Monitoring Data Reader for protected tables), and Foundry resources (Foundry User). Assign the narrowest role at the scope where the data lives.
rationale: User1 needs cost and usage charges only. Cost Management Reader grants read access to Cost Management data at the assigned scope, here the resource group, without any permission to change resources.

User2 needs quota usage across the subscription. Cognitive Services Usages Reader is the minimal role for viewing quota usage and must be assigned at subscription scope, because the Usages API is subscription-scoped.

User3 needs to read traces. Log Analytics Reader on the connected Application Insights resource allows viewing trace data; Privileged Monitoring Data Reader is needed in addition only when the tables are protected.
notes: Cost Management Reader: read access to cost and usage data. Use it for finance and chargeback reporting at subscription or resource group scope; it grants no access to resources or telemetry.
Cognitive Services Usages Reader: minimal read access to quota usage at subscription scope. Use it for capacity planning and to see quota allocations in the Foundry portal.
Log Analytics Reader: read access to monitoring data and logs. Assign it on the connected Application Insights resource so that users can view Foundry traces.
Foundry User: access to Foundry resources and projects to build and use agents. Assign it in addition to Cost Management Reader when users must also inspect Foundry resources and usage context.
Privileged Monitoring Data Reader: read access to protected Log Analytics tables. Use it when sensitive trace content, such as prompts in AppGenAIContent, is stored in a protected table.

stem:
Relecloud plans capacity for several agents that use gpt-4o. Before the team creates deployments, an architect must explain how Azure OpenAI Standard quota is granted.

Which scope should the architect use to plan Azure OpenAI quota?
choices: Per Azure OpenAI resource, shared by the deployments in that resource
Per subscription, per region, per model, and per deployment type
Per Microsoft Entra tenant, shared by every subscription in the tenant
Per Foundry project, shared by the deployments in that project
explanation: Quota planning starts at the subscription and region: each model and deployment type has a TPM pool there, and deployments take their share from it. To add capacity, redistribute TPM between deployments, request an increase, or use another region or subscription.
rationale: Incorrect: Azure OpenAI resources do not receive their own quota. Several resources in the same region and subscription draw from one quota pool, so planning per resource overstates capacity. Plan per resource only for the deployments that it hosts.
Correct: Standard quota is assigned in tokens per minute per subscription, per region, per model, and per deployment type. Each deployment takes part of that pool until the pool is used up.

Incorrect: quota is not pooled at the Microsoft Entra tenant level. Each subscription has its own quota per region and model, so a second subscription has a separate pool. Use more subscriptions when one subscription's quota is not enough.

Incorrect: Foundry projects do not receive their own Azure OpenAI quota. Deployments in all projects use the quota of the subscription in that region. Use projects to organize work and chargeback, not to obtain capacity.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank wants a monthly budget for resource group RG1, which hosts its Foundry resources. When spending reaches 80 percent of the budget, an existing Logic Apps workflow must start. Your Azure CLI session uses a different default subscription than the one that contains RG1.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `az account set --subscription <subscription-id>`
Run `az monitor action-group create --name AG1 --resource-group RG1 --short-name AG1` with an action that starts the Logic Apps workflow.

`az consumption budget create-with-rg --budget-name Budget1 -g RG1 --amount 10000 --category Cost --time-grain Monthly --time-period <period> --notifications <threshold-80-with-AG1-id-in-contact-groups>`
`az monitor metrics alert create --name Spend80 --resource-group RG1 --scopes <Foundry1-id> --condition "total ProcessedPromptTokens > 1000000" --action <AG1-id>`
`az cognitiveservices usage list --location eastus`
explanation: Azure OpenAI has no hard spending cap, so cost control relies on Cost Management budgets with alert thresholds. Budget notifications can call action groups, which start automation such as Logic Apps, Azure Functions, or runbooks; create the action group first so that the budget can reference it.
rationale: Step 1: az account set makes the subscription that contains RG1 the active one. The action group and the budget are created in the active subscription, so this must run before either command.

Step 2: the action group holds the action that starts the Logic Apps workflow. The budget notification references the action group ID in contact-groups, so the action group must exist before the budget is created.

Step 3: az consumption budget create-with-rg creates the monthly cost budget for RG1. Its notification with an 80 percent threshold and the AG1 ID in contact-groups starts the workflow when spending reaches that level.

Incorrect: a metric alert on processed prompt tokens reacts to token volume, not to money spent against a budget, and it ignores other cost meters. Use token alerts to watch usage spikes and budgets to watch spend.
Incorrect: az cognitiveservices usage list shows quota usage per region, which matters for capacity planning. It neither tracks spending nor triggers automation. Run it when you plan TPM allocations.

stem:
Contoso, Ltd. has three internal teams that call the same Azure OpenAI deployment from one Foundry project through Azure API Management. Each team sends a team identifier in an x-team-id header. Finance needs monthly token consumption per team for internal chargeback.

What should you configure?
choices: The llm-token-limit policy with a counter-key based on the x-team-id header
A cost analysis filter on the project tag
A metric alert on Processed Prompt Tokens split by deployment
The llm-emit-token-metric policy with a custom dimension based on the x-team-id header
