explanation: When consumers share a project and a deployment, platform cost data cannot tell them apart. The gateway sees every request, so API Management llm-emit-token-metric with a team dimension produces per-consumer token data for chargeback; keep the dimensions low in cardinality.
rationale: Incorrect: llm-token-limit enforces a token budget per key and rejects excess requests. It controls consumption but produces no per-team metric to report. Use it to cap usage per team, next to a metric policy for reporting.
Incorrect: the project tag splits cost by Foundry project. All three teams use one project, so the tag returns one total. Use the project tag when each team has its own project.

Incorrect: a metric alert split by deployment notifies on token thresholds per deployment. The teams share one deployment, so the split cannot separate them, and an alert is not a report. Use deployment splits when teams have separate deployments.

Correct: llm-emit-token-metric sends prompt, completion, and total token counts to Application Insights with custom dimensions such as the x-team-id header value, so finance can sum tokens per team each month.

stem:
Northwind Traders gives each partner a monthly allowance of 5 million tokens for an agent API in Azure API Management. When a partner exceeds its allowance, requests must be rejected until the next month starts. Partners use separate subscription keys.

Which configuration should you use?
choices: A separate TPM allocation for each partner on the shared Azure OpenAI deployment
llm-token-limit with token-quota and a Monthly token-quota-period per subscription ID
quota-by-key with calls and renewal-period, keyed on the subscription ID
llm-token-limit with a tokens-per-minute rate limit, keyed on the subscription ID
explanation: llm-token-limit has two modes: tokens-per-minute rate limiting (429 on excess) and token-quota over a period from Hourly to Yearly (403 until reset). Keying on the subscription ID applies the limit per partner, which is the basis for allowance-based plans.
rationale: Incorrect: a TPM allocation sets the rate limit of a whole deployment, which all partners share. It cannot give each partner a monthly allowance. Use TPM allocation to divide subscription quota among deployments.

Correct: llm-token-limit with token-quota and a Monthly token-quota-period, keyed on the subscription ID, counts each partner's tokens over the month and rejects requests with 403 Forbidden until the quota resets.

Incorrect: quota-by-key counts calls per key over a renewal period. A partner that sends few but large requests would exceed its token allowance unnoticed. Use it when the allowance is defined in calls.
Incorrect: a tokens-per-minute limit resets every minute, so a partner can keep consuming tokens all month. It throttles bursts, not monthly totals. Use it to protect capacity from runaway callers.

stem:
Adventure Works Cycles has 240,000 TPM of gpt-4o Standard quota in East US. Two deployments of gpt-4o version 2024-11-20 in a resource named Foundry1, Deployment1 and Deployment2, use 120,000 TPM each. Azure Monitor shows that Deployment2 uses less than 10 percent of its allocation. A new agent needs a gpt-4o Standard deployment named Deployment3 in Foundry1 with 60,000 TPM today, and a quota increase cannot be approved in time. You must confirm that the freed quota is available before you create Deployment3. The Azure CLI uses the correct subscription.

Which three actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: In the Foundry portal, open the Quota pane and lower the quota allocation of Deployment2 to 60,000 TPM.
`az cognitiveservices usage list -l eastus`

`az cognitiveservices account deployment create -g RG1 -n Foundry1 --deployment-name Deployment3 --model-name gpt-4o --model-version "2024-11-20" --model-format OpenAI --sku-capacity 60 --sku-name "Standard"`
`az cognitiveservices account create --name Foundry2 --resource-group RG1 --kind AIServices --sku S0 --location eastus`

`az cognitiveservices account deployment create -g RG1 -n Foundry1 --deployment-name Deployment3 --model-name gpt-4o --model-version "2024-11-20" --model-format OpenAI --sku-capacity 60000 --sku-name "Standard"`
explanation: Standard quota is a regional pool per subscription and model that deployments draw from in units of 1,000 TPM. When the pool is exhausted, lower the capacity of underused deployments to free quota, check usage, and then create the new deployment.
rationale: Step 1: once the regional pool is fully allocated, a new deployment needs TPM that another deployment of the same model releases. Editing the allocation of the underused Deployment2 on the Quota pane lowers it to 60,000 TPM and frees 60,000 TPM of the East US gpt-4o quota.

Step 2: az cognitiveservices usage list -l eastus shows quota usage in the region for the active subscription. Quota edits can take up to 15 minutes to propagate, so this check confirms that 60,000 TPM of gpt-4o Standard quota is free before Deployment3 is created.
Step 3: with quota freed, creating Deployment3 with --sku-capacity 60 assigns 60,000 TPM, because one capacity unit equals 1,000 TPM for Standard deployments.

Incorrect: a new resource in East US draws from the same subscription quota for gpt-4o Standard in that region, which is fully allocated. Create another resource when you need separate endpoints or keys, not more quota.
Incorrect: --sku-capacity is expressed in units of 1,000 TPM, so 60000 requests 60 million TPM, far beyond the available quota, and the deployment fails. Use 60 to request 60,000 TPM.

stem:
Alpine Ski House deployed a fine-tuned Azure OpenAI model that the marketing agent uses during one-week campaigns that run every other week. Cost analysis shows a steady charge for the model every day, including weeks with no inference calls.

What should you do to reduce this cost?
choices: Delete the deployment after each campaign and redeploy it before the next one
Reduce the TPM assigned to the fine-tuned deployment between campaigns
Configure spillover from the fine-tuned deployment to a standard deployment
Add an llm-token-limit policy with a monthly token quota for the marketing agent
explanation: Fine-tuned models have three cost components: training, inference per token, and hourly hosting while deployed. Hosting accrues even when the model is idle, so for periodic workloads delete deployments between uses.
rationale: Correct: a deployed fine-tuned model incurs an hourly hosting charge as long as it is deployed, even without inference calls. Deleting the deployment after each campaign and redeploying before the next stops the idle charge.

Incorrect: TPM sets the rate limit of the deployment and affects how many tokens it can process. It does not change the hourly hosting charge of a fine-tuned deployment. Reduce TPM to free quota for other deployments.

Incorrect: spillover routes overflow from a provisioned deployment to a standard deployment. It does not apply to idle fine-tuned hosting and does not lower the hourly charge. Use spillover to absorb PTU peaks.
Incorrect: a monthly token quota limits inference consumption by the agent. The charge appears in weeks without inference, so it is hosting, not tokens. Use a token quota to cap usage-based spending.

stem:
You review the token metric issue that is described in the Problem statements section.

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: Token data for some requests is discarded without an error being returned to the caller.
Adding Client IP as a fourth custom dimension reduces the amount of discarded token data.
Removing the User ID dimension makes the per-cost-center totals complete.
explanation: Custom metrics from API Management create active time series as the product of the unique values of each dimension, with limits of 100 values per dimension and 1,000 series per namespace. Use low-cardinality dimensions such as cost center or API for chargeback, and handle per-user analysis in logs instead of metrics.
rationale: Yes: API Management limits each dimension to 100 unique values and each metric namespace to 1,000 active time series. With 4,000 users, new User ID values exceed the limits, and that metric data is silently discarded, with no error to callers.

No: Client IP is another high-cardinality dimension. The number of time series is the product of the unique values of each dimension, so adding it multiplies the series count and makes data loss worse. Add only dimensions with few values.

Yes: without User ID, the series count is 3 APIs times 40 cost centers, or 120, well under the 1,000 limit, and each dimension stays under 100 values, so every request counts toward the cost center totals.

stem:
Coho Winery wants to reduce billing surprises before it moves a multi-agent solution to production. You need to estimate costs and verify the estimate against actual charges before you set the production budget.

Which four actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: Build an estimate in the Azure pricing calculator.
Deploy a small test workload and send representative traffic.
Group costs by Resource and then by Meter in Cost analysis.
Compare the meter charges with the estimate and adjust the budget.
Create a scheduled export of cost data to a storage account.
Enable a diagnostic setting that sends Foundry resource metrics to a Log Analytics workspace.
explanation: Microsoft recommends an estimate-and-verify approach: estimate with the pricing calculator, run a representative test, break the actual cost down by resource and meter, and adjust the budget. Meters are the unit at which estimates and invoices can be compared.
rationale: Step 1: the pricing calculator turns the expected models, token volumes, and other services into a baseline estimate. The baseline must exist first, because the later steps verify it.
Step 2: a small test workload with representative traffic produces real charges on the actual meters. Without it, Cost analysis has no data that reflects the planned usage.
Step 3: grouping by Resource and then by Meter breaks the test charges down to priced units, such as input and output tokens per model, which is the level at which the estimate was built.
Step 4: comparing the meter charges with the estimate shows which assumptions were wrong, so you can correct the baseline and set a realistic production budget.

Incorrect: a scheduled export copies cost data to storage for reporting or external tools. It neither estimates nor verifies anything by itself. Use it when finance needs regular cost data outside the portal.

Incorrect: a diagnostic setting sends platform metrics and logs for operational monitoring. They are not billing data, and Log Analytics ingestion adds its own cost. Use it for availability and performance monitoring.

stem:
Wide World Importers enabled spillover from a Global Provisioned deployment to a Global Standard deployment. Finance reports pay-as-you-go token charges that are higher than expected and asks the team to identify how much of the Global Standard traffic arrived through spillover.

Which two actions should you perform? Each correct answer presents a complete solution.
choices: Log the x-ms-spillover-from-deployment response header in the agent application and count the requests that contain it
Count the HTTP 429 responses of the provisioned deployment in the Azure OpenAI Requests metric
Group cost analysis by Meter for the Foundry resource
Split the Azure OpenAI Requests metric of the Global Standard deployment by the IsSpillover dimension
Chart the Provisioned-managed Utilization V2 metric of the provisioned deployment
explanation: Spilled requests are billed on the standard deployment at standard rates, so they show up as pay-as-you-go charges. Measure them with the IsSpillover dimension on the request metric of the standard deployment, or per request with the x-ms-spillover-from-deployment header.
rationale: Correct: the x-ms-spillover-from-deployment response header is present on requests that were served through spillover. Logging and counting it in the application gives a per-request count of spilled traffic.

Incorrect: requests that spill over are served by the standard deployment instead of returning 429, so they are not counted as 429 responses on the provisioned deployment. Count 429 responses when spillover is not enabled.

Incorrect: grouping by Meter shows token charges per model and token type, but spilled and direct requests to the Global Standard deployment use the same meters. Use meter grouping to see which models drive cost.
Correct: the Azure OpenAI Requests metric of the Global Standard deployment can be split by the IsSpillover dimension, which separates requests that arrived through spillover from direct requests.
Incorrect: Provisioned-managed Utilization V2 shows how full the provisioned deployment is. High utilization explains why spillover happens but does not count spilled requests. Use it to size PTUs.

stem:
Graphic Design Institute scopes Cost analysis to its Foundry resource to track the cost of a tutoring agent. The agent uses Azure OpenAI models and a partner model from Azure Marketplace, and tracing sends telemetry to Application Insights. The monthly invoice is consistently higher than the Foundry resource view shows.

What should you do to see the full cost of the solution?
choices: Wait for cost ingestion and compare the same time window again
Scope Cost analysis to the resource group or subscription of the solution
Add a filter for the Azure OpenAI service in the Foundry resource view
Assign the Cost Management Reader role at the Foundry resource scope
explanation: Foundry costs are only part of a solution's cost: Marketplace partner models, Application Insights and Log Analytics, and other services are billed outside the Foundry resource. Analyze cost at the resource group or subscription that contains all resources of the solution.
rationale: Incorrect: cost data can lag, but the difference here is the same every month, so it is structural, not a timing issue. Wait and compare again when only the most recent day looks too low.

Correct: meters for partner models from Azure Marketplace appear at the resource group instead of the Foundry resource, and Azure Monitor costs for logs and alerts belong to other resources. Scoping to the resource group or subscription shows all of them.

Incorrect: a service filter narrows the view and hides even more of the solution cost. The gap comes from costs outside the Foundry resource scope. Use filters to isolate one service once the scope is complete.

Incorrect: the user can already see the Foundry resource costs, so permissions are not the issue; the missing costs sit outside this scope. Assign Cost Management Reader at a wider scope only when access is denied.

stem:
Fabrikam, Inc. has a planning agent whose runs include several model calls and tool calls. A developer needs to identify which model call in one specific run consumed the most tokens and how long each step took.

What should the developer use?
choices: The Processed Prompt Tokens metric of the model deployment in Azure Monitor
The trace of the run in the Foundry portal, stepping through each span
The token usage chart on the Agent Monitoring Dashboard of the agent
Cost analysis in Cost Management, grouped by Meter for the project
explanation: Tracing records each run as a tree of spans with timing, tokens, inputs, and outputs, which is the level needed for per-step diagnosis. Metrics and dashboards aggregate across runs and suit trends and alerts, not the explanation of one run.
rationale: Incorrect: Processed Prompt Tokens aggregates input tokens across requests over time. It cannot attribute tokens to one run or one model call, and it covers input only. Use it to watch prompt volume trends per deployment.

Correct: a trace in the Foundry portal shows each model call and tool call of the run as a span with its inputs, outputs, token usage, and duration in execution order, so you can find the most expensive call and the slow steps.

Incorrect: the token usage chart on the Agent Monitoring Dashboard aggregates tokens across runs over a period. It does not break one run into steps. Use it to spot trends and anomalies in consumption.
Incorrect: Cost analysis shows billed charges per meter and resource over days, not tokens per step of an individual run. Use it for cost reporting and chargeback.

stem:
Litware, Inc. instruments a Python agent application with the Microsoft Foundry SDK. Tracing is already enabled and spans appear in Application Insights. In the development environment, developers need the built-in traces to include message contents and tool call arguments.

Which environment variable should you set to true?
choices: AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INCLUDE_BINARY_DATA
OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT
AZURE_EXPERIMENTAL_ENABLE_GENAI_TRACING
AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_TRACE_CONTEXT_PROPAGATION_INCLUDE_BAGGAGE
explanation: Foundry SDK tracing has separate switches: enable tracing, record content, propagate trace context and baggage, auto-instrument the Responses API, and include binary data. Content recording can expose sensitive data, so enable it in development unless compliance allows it in production.
rationale: Incorrect: AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INCLUDE_BINARY_DATA adds full image URLs and file data to spans, and it applies only when content recording is already on. It does not enable message content. Use it when you must debug multimodal inputs.

Correct: OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT set to true turns on content recording, so built-in spans capture message contents and tool call arguments. It is off by default and intended for development.

Incorrect: AZURE_EXPERIMENTAL_ENABLE_GENAI_TRACING opts in to GenAI tracing itself. Spans already appear, so tracing is on, and this variable adds no content. Set it when no GenAI spans are produced at all.

Incorrect: AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_TRACE_CONTEXT_PROPAGATION_INCLUDE_BAGGAGE adds the baggage header to the propagated trace context. It changes what is sent to Azure services, not what spans record. Enable it only when downstream services need baggage.

stem:
Tailspin Toys wants Foundry to notify the team when the token usage or latency of an agent shows an anomaly, or when evaluation scores drop.

Which setting on the Monitor tab of the agent should you configure?
choices: Red team scans
Recurring evaluations
Traces
Alerts
explanation: The Monitor tab combines recurring evaluations and red team scans, which produce signals, with alerts, which notify on anomalies in those signals and in operational metrics. Traces support the investigation after an alert fires.
rationale: Incorrect: red team scans run adversarial probes against the agent to find safety risks. Their findings can feed alerts, but the scans do not notify on latency or token anomalies. Use them to test safety on a schedule.
Incorrect: recurring evaluations produce quality scores over time. They supply the data that an alert watches, but they do not send notifications themselves. Use them to measure quality regularly.
Incorrect: Traces show individual runs for debugging, including spans and tokens. They contain no notification settings. Use traces to investigate a specific run after an alert fires.

Correct: Alerts in the Monitor settings of the agent detect anomalies in latency, token usage, evaluation scores, and red team findings and notify the team, which covers every condition in the requirement.

stem:
Relecloud connected an Application Insights resource to its Foundry project. A developer named User1 has the Contributor role on the project but receives authorization errors when opening traces in the Foundry portal. The trace tables are not protected.

Which role should you assign to User1 on the connected Application Insights resource?
choices: Log Analytics Reader
Privileged Monitoring Data Reader
Cost Management Reader
Cognitive Services Usages Reader
explanation: Trace data lives in the connected Application Insights resource, so access to it is controlled there, not on the Foundry project. Log Analytics Reader covers standard tables; protected tables additionally need Privileged Monitoring Data Reader.
rationale: Correct: viewing traces requires Log Analytics Reader on the Application Insights resource connected to the project, in addition to a role on the project. Contributor on the project alone does not grant read access to the telemetry.

Incorrect: Privileged Monitoring Data Reader grants access to protected Log Analytics tables. The trace tables are not protected, so it is not needed. Assign it in addition when sensitive content is stored in a protected table.
Incorrect: Cost Management Reader grants read access to cost and usage charges. It provides no access to Application Insights telemetry. Assign it to users who need cost reports.
Incorrect: Cognitive Services Usages Reader shows quota usage at subscription scope. It grants no access to trace data. Assign it to users who plan TPM capacity.

stem:
Woodgrove Bank calls a Foundry agent from a Python application that is instrumented for tracing. Traces reach Application Insights, but they are not correlated with the agent in the Foundry portal.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
response = openai.responses.create(
    conversation=conversation.id,
    extra_body={"agent_reference": {
        "name": [[1]],
        "id": [[2]],
        "type": "agent_reference",
    }},
    input="What is my current balance?",
)
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Correct: the name key must hold the agent name. Together with the id, it tells the Foundry portal which agent the client-side traces belong to, so they appear under that agent.
Incorrect: agent.version identifies one version of the agent, not its name. Pass the version when you manage a specific agent version, for example with delete_version.
Incorrect: conversation.id identifies the conversation that holds the turns and is already passed in the conversation parameter. It does not identify the agent.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Correct: Microsoft Learn requires both name and id in agent_reference to correlate traces with a specific agent. agent.id supplies the identifier that was returned when the agent version was created.
Incorrect: agent.version is a version label, not the agent identifier that agent_reference expects for correlation. Use it when you manage agent versions.

Incorrect: conversation.id would point the reference at a conversation instead of the agent, so the portal still cannot correlate the traces with the agent. Pass it in the conversation parameter only.

explanation: Client-side traces are linked to a Foundry agent through agent_reference in the responses.create() call, which must include both the agent name and the agent id. Traces usually appear within 2 to 5 minutes after the call.

stem:
You need to meet the session correlation requirement for TripPlanner.

How should you complete the code? To answer, select the appropriate options in the answer area.

```python
from typing import cast
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import SpanProcessor, TracerProvider

class SessionSpanProcessor(SpanProcessor):
    def [[1]](self, span, parent_context=None):
        [[2]]

    def on_end(self, span):
        pass

provider = cast(TracerProvider, trace.get_tracer_provider())
[[3]]
```

targets.label: Box 1
why: Correct: on_start runs when each span starts, while the span is still writable, so an attribute set there is present on every span, including spans created by the Foundry SDK instrumentation.
Incorrect: on_end receives a read-only span after it has finished, so attributes can no longer be added. Use on_end to inspect or export completed spans.
Incorrect: force_flush asks the processor to export buffered spans immediately and is not called for each span. Use it before the process exits so that pending spans are not lost.

targets.label: Box 2
why: Correct: set_attribute adds session.id as an attribute of the span, which is what the requirement asks for and what KQL queries and the Foundry portal can filter on.
Incorrect: add_event records a timestamped event inside the span, not an attribute of the span, so filtering spans by session.id does not work. Use events to mark moments within a span.

Incorrect: set_baggage places the value in a context that propagates to downstream services; it does not set a span attribute, and propagated baggage can leak data. Use baggage for non-sensitive cross-service context.

targets.label: Box 3
why: Correct: add_span_processor registers the processor with the global tracer provider that the application and the SDK instrumentation already use, so every new span passes through on_start.

Incorrect: setting a new TracerProvider does not register the processor, and the new provider lacks the configured exporter, so spans would neither get the attribute nor reach Application Insights. Use it only at startup when no provider exists.
Incorrect: force_flush exports pending spans but registers nothing, so spans never pass through SessionSpanProcessor. Call it during shutdown to flush telemetry.

explanation: A SpanProcessor registered with the global tracer provider sees every span that starts in the process, including spans from SDK instrumentation. Setting attributes in on_start adds correlation IDs such as session.id without changing the traced functions.

stem:
Northwind Traders has two agent applications, App1 and App2, that send OpenTelemetry traces to the same Application Insights resource. The team needs to filter the traces of each application in KQL queries without creating another Application Insights resource.

What should you do?
choices: Set a unique OTEL_SERVICE_NAME for each application and filter on cloud_RoleName
Create a separate Foundry project for each application that shares the resource
Add a session.id attribute that identifies the application to every span
Set the gen_ai.operation.name attribute to the application name on each span
explanation: Within a shared Application Insights resource, component identity comes from the OpenTelemetry service name, stored as cloud_RoleName. Use it to filter queries and to show separate nodes in Application map, and keep session and operation attributes for their own purposes.
rationale: Correct: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME sets the OpenTelemetry service name, which Application Insights maps to cloud_RoleName. A unique value per app lets KQL queries filter each application in the shared resource.

Incorrect: a separate Foundry project per application changes how the apps are organized, but both still send telemetry to the same Application Insights resource with no field that tells them apart. Use separate projects for access or chargeback boundaries.

Incorrect: session.id identifies a user session, which spans one conversation, not an application. Reusing it for app identity breaks session correlation. Use session.id to group the spans of one session.

Incorrect: gen_ai.operation.name describes the operation of a span, such as chat or execute_tool, according to the GenAI semantic conventions. Overloading it breaks those conventions. Use it to filter spans by operation type.

stem:
Proseware, Inc. adds client-side tracing to a Python agent application that uses the Microsoft Foundry SDK. Client-side spans must be produced for every agent call and must correlate with server-side spans from Azure OpenAI. The startup code already calls configure_azure_monitor() with the connection string of the Application Insights resource of the project.

Which five actions should you perform in sequence? To answer, move the appropriate actions from the list of actions to the answer area and arrange them in the correct order.
choices: `pip install azure-ai-projects opentelemetry-sdk azure-core-tracing-opentelemetry azure-monitor-opentelemetry`
`os.environ["AZURE_EXPERIMENTAL_ENABLE_GENAI_TRACING"] = "true"`
`AIProjectInstrumentor().instrument()`
`openai = project.get_openai_client(agent_name=agent.name)`
`response = openai.responses.create(input=question)`
`os.environ["AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INSTRUMENT_RESPONSES_API"] = "false"`
`AIProjectInstrumentor().instrument(enable_trace_context_propagation=False)`
`pip install opentelemetry-exporter-otlp`
explanation: Foundry SDK tracing in Python follows a strict startup order: install the packages, opt in with AZURE_EXPERIMENTAL_ENABLE_GENAI_TRACING, call AIProjectInstrumentor().instrument(), and only then obtain OpenAI clients. Clients obtained before instrumentation do not propagate trace context.
rationale: Step 1: the packages provide the Foundry SDK, the OpenTelemetry SDK, the Azure Core tracing bridge, and the Azure Monitor exporter. They must be installed before any import or call in the later steps can run.
Step 2: GenAI tracing is an experimental opt-in. The variable must be true before instrument() is called; otherwise instrumentation is not enabled and only a warning is logged.
Step 3: instrument() enables the GenAI instrumentation, with trace context propagation on by default. It must run before the OpenAI client is obtained so that the client is covered.

Step 4: trace context propagation applies only to OpenAI clients obtained through get_openai_client() after instrumentation, so the client is obtained after instrument() to inject the traceparent and tracestate headers.
Step 5: calls through the instrumented client now produce client-side spans and carry the trace context to Azure OpenAI, so client-side and server-side spans correlate in one trace.

Incorrect: setting AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INSTRUMENT_RESPONSES_API to false disables automatic instrumentation of Responses and Conversations calls, so agent calls produce no client-side spans. Use it when you want only explicit custom spans.

Incorrect: instrument(enable_trace_context_propagation=False) stops injecting W3C trace context headers, so client-side and server-side spans no longer correlate. Use it when compliance forbids sending trace IDs to Azure services.

Incorrect: opentelemetry-exporter-otlp is needed to export to an OTLP backend such as Aspire Dashboard or a third-party tool. The app exports to Application Insights through configure_azure_monitor(), so this package is not required.

Humongous Insurance traces a claims agent in production. OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT is set to false. A helper function named lookup_policy is decorated with @trace_function and accepts a policy_number parameter. A compliance review finds policy numbers in the span attributes of production traces. The team must keep a span for lookup_policy.

What should you do?
choices: Set AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_ENABLE_TRACE_CONTEXT_PROPAGATION to false
Set AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INSTRUMENT_RESPONSES_API to false
Replace the decorator with a manual span that omits policy_number
Set AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INCLUDE_BINARY_DATA to false
explanation: Content recording controls only the built-in GenAI spans. The @trace_function decorator always records parameters as code.function.parameter attributes and the return value, so for sensitive parameters create a manual span with explicitly chosen attributes.
rationale: Incorrect: disabling trace context propagation stops sending traceparent headers to Azure services, which affects only correlation. The decorator still records policy_number as a span attribute. Disable propagation when trace IDs must not leave the app.

Incorrect: this variable disables automatic instrumentation of Responses and Conversations API calls. lookup_policy is a decorated custom function, so its span and parameters are still recorded. Use it when you want only explicit custom spans.

Correct: @trace_function records all supported parameters and the return value regardless of the content recording setting. A manual span created with the tracer lets you choose the attributes, so it keeps a span for lookup_policy without policy_number.

Incorrect: AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_INCLUDE_BINARY_DATA controls whether image and file data is included when content recording is on. Policy numbers are plain parameters, so the setting has no effect. Leave it false to keep payloads small.

Trey Research stores clinical prompts in Foundry traces. The September 30, 2026, migration date for generative AI content has passed. Earlier, the team registered the optOutProtectGenAISensitiveData feature flag on the subscription so that existing custom queries kept working, and all queries now read from the AppGenAIContent table. Members of an auditor group must be able to read prompts, responses, and tool call content in new traces, while other engineers keep access to the non-sensitive trace data only.

Which sequence of actions should you perform?
choices: Register the protectGenAISensitiveData feature flag -> set the AppGenAIContent table to Protected -> assign Privileged Monitoring Data Reader to the auditor group -> verify access with an account that has Log Analytics Reader

Unregister the optOutProtectGenAISensitiveData feature flag -> set the AppGenAIContent table to Protected -> assign Privileged Monitoring Data Reader to the auditor group -> verify access with an account that has Log Analytics Reader

Set the AppGenAIContent table to Protected -> assign Privileged Monitoring Data Reader to the auditor group -> verify access with an account that has Log Analytics Reader -> unregister the optOutProtectGenAISensitiveData feature flag

Unregister the optOutProtectGenAISensitiveData feature flag -> verify access with an account that has Log Analytics Reader -> set the AppGenAIContent table to Protected -> assign Privileged Monitoring Data Reader to the auditor group
explanation: Foundry stores sensitive GenAI attributes, such as input and output messages and tool call arguments, in the AppGenAIContent table. For data ingested on or after September 30, 2026, Application Insights routes these values only to AppGenAIContent by default, so the early-enablement flag protectGenAISensitiveData is no longer needed; only the temporary optOutProtectGenAISensitiveData flag keeps the old routing, until you unregister it or the opt-out ends on September 30, 2027. Then protect the table so that standard readers are denied, grant Privileged Monitoring Data Reader to authorized identities, and verify with both kinds of accounts.
rationale: Incorrect: protectGenAISensitiveData enabled the dedicated-table routing early, before the September 30, 2026, migration date. Now it adds nothing, and the registered opt-out flag still keeps content values in AppDependencies, AppTraces, and AppEvents, where a Log Analytics Reader can read them. Register it only before the migration date.

Correct: unregistering optOutProtectGenAISensitiveData returns new data to the default routing, so content values go only to AppGenAIContent. Protecting that table denies standard readers, Privileged Monitoring Data Reader restores access for the auditors, and the final check confirms both outcomes.

Incorrect: this order verifies while the opt-out flag still copies content values into the existing telemetry tables, so the Log Analytics Reader account can still read prompts and the check fails. Unregister the opt-out first, and verify only after the final configuration is in place.

Incorrect: verifying before the table is set to Protected shows that a Log Analytics Reader can still read the content, because unprotected tables follow standard read roles, and the auditors have no dedicated role yet. Protect the table and grant access before you verify.

Wingtip Toys deploys a hosted agent named Agent1 in Foundry Agent Service. Monitoring is enabled for the Foundry project, and the agent code contains no telemetry setup code. The agent version is deployed with this agent.yaml section:

```yaml
environment_variables:
  - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT
    value: https://otlp.example-provider.com
  - name: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL
    value: http/protobuf
  - name: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME
    value: booking-agent
```

For each of the following statements, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No.
choices: Agent1 sends telemetry to both the Application Insights resource of the project and the OTLP endpoint.
You can change the OTLP endpoint of the deployed agent version without creating a new agent version.
In Application Insights, the telemetry of Agent1 appears with booking-agent as the cloud_RoleName.
explanation: Hosted agents bundle the OpenTelemetry distro and choose exporters from environment variables at startup: Application Insights through the platform-injected connection string, and OTLP through OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT. Export settings are immutable per version, and service.name always equals the agent name.
rationale: Yes: with project monitoring enabled, Foundry injects APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING into the container, and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT adds an OTLP exporter. The two exporters are independent, so telemetry goes to both destinations.
No: environment variables are set per agent version and are immutable once the version is created. To change the export destination or the headers, you create a new agent version.

No: hosted agents report service.name fixed to the agent name, shown as cloud_RoleName, so the value is Agent1. The platform overrides OTEL_SERVICE_NAME; to use another service name, name the agent accordingly.

stem:
Margie's Travel enables Foundry SDK tracing in a Python application. Client-side spans and server-side spans from Azure OpenAI appear as separate traces. Trace context propagation is at its default value. During startup, the application obtains an OpenAI client by calling get_openai_client() and then calls AIProjectInstrumentor().instrument().

What should you do to correlate the spans?
choices: Obtain the OpenAI client by calling get_openai_client() after the instrumentation call
Call instrument() with enable_trace_context_propagation set to False
Set AZURE_TRACING_GEN_AI_TRACE_CONTEXT_PROPAGATION_INCLUDE_BAGGAGE to true
Set OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT to true
explanation: Trace context propagation is on by default when tracing is enabled, but it applies only to OpenAI clients obtained through get_openai_client() after instrumentation or after a setting change. The order of client creation therefore decides whether client and server spans join one trace.
rationale: Correct: trace context propagation injects traceparent and tracestate only into OpenAI clients obtained through get_openai_client() after instrumentation. Obtaining the client after instrument() makes its requests carry the context, so the spans correlate.

Incorrect: enable_trace_context_propagation=False turns off the header injection that correlates client-side and server-side spans, which is the opposite of the goal. Use it when compliance forbids sharing trace identifiers.

Incorrect: the baggage variable adds the baggage header with key-value pairs to the propagated context. It depends on propagation already working for the client, which it does not here, and it can expose PII. Use it only for non-sensitive data.

Incorrect: content recording adds message contents and tool arguments to spans. It does not add trace headers to requests, so the traces stay separate. Enable it in development when you need to see content.
